fixes.explanation: Being ignored is a real kind of lonely, but that's not what Jeremiah describes. He says he is a laughingstock and that everyone mocks him. Ignoring someone means looking past them. Mocking means aiming at them.

Avoiding someone means crossing the street to dodge them. Jeremiah describes something different. He says he is a laughingstock all day long, and that everyone mocks him. That's people making him the joke, not people dodging him.

A stone sounds heavy, and I think Jeremiah feels the weight of all this. But that's not the picture he uses. He says the message becomes a fire burning in his heart, shut up in his bones. A stone just sits there. A fire keeps burning.

A chain would hold him in place, but Jeremiah doesn't say that. He says the message becomes a fire burning in his heart, shut up in his bones. A chain stays still. A fire burns, and he says this one is shut up in his bones.

The prophets of Baal aren't mentioned anywhere in these verses. The ones watching for his fall are named right there. Jeremiah says, “All my trusted friends watch for my fall…” Those are people he trusted.
Jeremiah doesn't say that. He says, “…my persecutors will stumble and will not prevail.” He pictures them tripping and losing. Nobody switches sides in that verse.
Moving away isn't what Jeremiah says here. He says, “…my persecutors will stumble and will not prevail.” What he describes is stumbling and not prevailing.

The text says the opposite. Jeremiah calls the LORD of Hosts the One “…who sees the heart and mind…” He says it in the same prayer where he commits his cause to Him. Those are his own words in verse 12.

That's what comes out of him. Jeremiah calls out, “Sing to the LORD! Praise the LORD!” It comes right after he commits his cause to the LORD. After the mockery and whispering earlier in the passage, I think it's a quick swing, and I love how honest it is.
Running isn't in the text. Right after committing his cause to the LORD, Jeremiah calls out, “Sing to the LORD! Praise the LORD!” He's not hiding. He's calling for praise.
Jeremiah is not quiet here. He calls out, “Sing to the LORD! Praise the LORD!” After his appeal to the LORD, it's a loud turn. Nothing about waiting in silence.
Worry isn't in the verse. Jeremiah says the man brought his father the news, “bringing him great joy.” His father got a happy message, and Jeremiah curses the man who brought it.

Those cities. Jeremiah says, “May that man be like the cities that the LORD overthrew without compassion.” He doesn't name them here, so I won't guess which ones he means. That's the picture he gives.
A watchman isn't in these verses. Jeremiah says, “May that man be like the cities that the LORD overthrew without compassion.” He's comparing the man to overthrown cities.
Trouble and sorrow. Jeremiah asks why he came out of the womb “…to see only trouble and sorrow…” It's a question, and it comes straight from the heart. I think he's saying exactly how it feels.
Honor and riches aren't in his question. Jeremiah asks why he came out of the womb “…to see only trouble and sorrow…” That's what he says he sees. Trouble and sorrow are the words he uses.
